teacher_notes.primer: This opening Key Stage 2 enquiry introduces Britain’s earliest written legal system under Roman rule (AD 43–410). Pupils investigate how written laws rooted in Rome’s Twelve Tables were judged by town magistrates inside stone basilicas, why the absence of a detective police force meant ordinary victims had to catch suspects themselves, how punishments differed sharply between wealthy Roman citizens and enslaved people, and why bathers at Aquae Sulis (Bath) threw over 130 scratched lead curse tablets to goddess Sulis Minerva.

items.question: Put these three eras of British history into the right order, starting with the earliest: Victorians, Roman Britain, Tudors.
items.answer: Roman Britain, then the Tudors, then the Victorians
items.explanation: Roman Britain began in AD 43, the Tudors ruled from 1485, and Queen Victoria reigned from 1837!

items.question: Why is it fairer for a town to write its laws down clearly instead of keeping them secret?
items.answer: Everyone knows the rules in advance, and judges cannot simply invent unfair rules to help their friends
items.explanation: Written rules help protect ordinary families from sudden, made-up punishments.

items.question: Today, who can you phone on 999 if someone steals from a shop or house?
items.answer: The police service
items.explanation: Modern Britain has paid, trained police officers—something ancient and medieval Britain did not have!

items.question: What is the difference between a "crime" and a "punishment"?
items.answer: A crime is an action that breaks the law, while a punishment is the penalty given by a court
items.explanation: Across 2,000 years, new laws created new crimes and courts changed how offenders were punished.

items.question: Before the Romans invaded Britain in AD 43, how did Iron Age tribes pass on their customs and rules?
items.answer: By spoken word and memory rather than written law books
items.explanation: Iron Age Britain had skilled craftworkers and hillforts, but Rome brought Britain’s first written law codes.

narrative_blocks.title: AD 43–200: Written Twelve Tables and Basilica Magistrates
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.1] After **AD 43**, **Roman** governors brought Britain’s first **written laws**, shaped by Rome’s ancient **Twelve Tables**. In towns like **Londinium**, officials displayed clear rules on wooden and bronze boards so traders knew what was legal. Written rules stopped local chiefs making up unfair laws on the spot.

[1.2] Serious crimes were judged inside a grand stone hall called a **basilica** [buh-SIL-ih-kuh] beside the market forum. There a senior judge called a **magistrate** [MAJ-ih-strayt] weighed witness evidence, checked bronze market scales, and ordered lawful fines or sentences.

narrative_blocks.title: AD 43–300: No Police Force and Unequal Roman Ranks
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.3] Surprisingly, **Roman Britain** had **no police force** to investigate everyday thefts! **Roman legionaries** [lee-juh-NAIR-eez] guarded forts and roads, while town **vigiles** [VIJ-ih-leez] patrolled dark streets with water buckets to spot fires. Ordinary victims had to chase and catch suspects themselves!

[1.4] Roman courts also punished people unequally by social rank. Wealthy **Roman citizens** usually paid money **fines** or faced **exile** abroad, whereas **enslaved people** had no rights and suffered harsh **whipping**, hard labour in dark mines, or death in the **amphitheatre**.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 100–400: Stolen Cloaks and Lead Curse Tablets at Bath
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.5] What could a bather do if nobody saw who snatched their warm wool cloak? At **Aquae Sulis** [AK-way SOO-liss], now **Bath**, busy bathers left tunics, rings, and coins on stone benches beside steaming green pools.

[1.6] Furious victims bought thin sheets of soft grey **lead** called **curse tablets** and scratched Latin pleas with a sharp iron pen. Folding each tablet tightly, they dropped it into the hot spring, begging goddess **Sulis Minerva** to punish the thief until their stolen goods came back!

tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, robbed bathers at Aquae Sulis scratched curses onto folded lead sheets because...

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain why written Roman laws were an important step forward, yet still not fair for everyone.
tasks.starter: Written Roman laws were an important step forward for Britain, yet they were not fair for everyone because...
hints: Explain why written rules based on the Twelve Tables helped townspeople before a magistrate.
Compare the lighter fines or exile given to wealthy Roman citizens.
Contrast this with the harsh whipping, mine labour, or amphitheatre punishments given to enslaved people.
tasks.model_answer: Written Roman laws were an important step forward for Britain, yet they were not fair for everyone because social rank decided your punishment. Displaying rules based on the Twelve Tables stopped a magistrate making up secret laws, and wealthy Roman citizens usually paid money fines or faced exile. However, enslaved people had far fewer rights and suffered cruel whipping, mine labour, or execution in the amphitheatre.

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: How did the Romans catch thieves and judge crimes in Britain without a police force?
tasks.starter: Between AD 43 and AD 410, Roman towns judged crimes using written rules, yet catching thieves relied on ordinary people because...
hints: Explain what legionaries and night-watch vigiles actually did—and who had to catch everyday thieves.
Describe what happened inside the stone basilica once a suspect was brought before a magistrate.
Show how robbed bathers at Bath turned to Sulis Minerva when thieves escaped unseen!
tasks.model_answer: Between AD 43 and AD 410, Roman towns judged crimes using written rules, yet catching thieves relied on ordinary people because legionaries guarded forts and night-watch vigiles mainly watched for fires. Victims had to catch suspects themselves and bring them to a magistrate in the stone basilica, where Roman citizens paid fines while enslaved people faced harsh penalties—and whenever thieves escaped unseen at Bath, victims dropped lead curses to Sulis Minerva!

narrative_blocks.title: AD 410–900: Ten-Person Tithings and the Hue and Cry
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.1] After Roman rule ended around **AD 410**, **Anglo-Saxon** families farmed around small timber villages with **no prisons** and **no police**. Instead, every male villager aged **twelve** and over joined a group of ten neighbours called a **tithing** [TY-thing].

[2.2] If one member broke the **King’s Peace**, the other nine men had to bring him to court or pay a fine! Anyone spotting a crime blew a horn and shouted the **Hue and Cry**, forcing every villager in earshot to chase the thief.

narrative_blocks.title: c. AD 600–900: King Alfred’s Laws and Silver Wergild
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.3] Early on, an injury could spark a deadly **blood feud** as rival families took revenge. To keep peace, rulers from **King Aethelberht** to **King Alfred the Great** wrote Old English law codes fixing silver compensation called **wergild** [WER-gild], meaning **"person-price"**.

[2.4] Every body part and social rank carried an exact silver value! Yet **wergild** was unequal: a noble **thane** was worth **1,200 shillings**, six times a free **ceorl** [CHURL] farmer at **200 shillings**. **Repeat traitors** or coin-forgers still faced hanging or losing a hand.

narrative_blocks.title: AD 600–1066: Hundred Courts and Trial by Ordeal
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.5] Each month, **Anglo-Saxon** elders met outdoors at the **Hundred Court**, where respected neighbours called **oath-helpers** swore before God that a suspect spoke truthfully. Only when witnesses still could not tell who lied did priests hold **Trial by Ordeal** inside a stone church.

[2.6] In **Trial by Hot Iron**, the suspect carried a glowing iron bar **three paces** and had their burned hand bandaged for **three days**. A clean healing burn meant **God** declared them innocent, while a festering wound—or floating in blessed **cold water**—meant guilty!

tasks.question: Study Source A. Why did Anglo-Saxon kings write down exact shilling fines for every injury?
tasks.starter: Looking at Source A, Anglo-Saxon kings wrote down exact shilling fines in Old English because...
hints: Explain what violent problem happened when injured families took revenge with weapons.
Define wergild ("person-price") and how silver shillings compensated the victim’s family.
Note whether every rank (noble thane vs ceorl farmer) had the same shilling value!
tasks.model_answer: Looking at Source A, Anglo-Saxon kings wrote down exact shilling fines in Old English because clear wergild ("person-price") payments stopped angry families starting deadly blood feuds. Instead of taking violent revenge, wrongdoers paid silver shillings to the victim’s kin—although a noble thane’s 1,200-shilling wergild was worth six times a ceorl farmer’s 200 shillings!

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain how Anglo-Saxon villagers caught lawbreakers without having paid police officers.
tasks.starter: Without paid police officers, Anglo-Saxon villages relied on every neighbour to keep order by...
hints: Describe the ten-person tithing joined by every male villager aged twelve and over.
Explain what happened if one member broke the law and ran away.
Show how shouting the Hue and Cry brought suspects before the monthly Hundred Court.
tasks.model_answer: Without paid police officers, Anglo-Saxon villages relied on every neighbour to keep order by placing every male aged twelve and over into a ten-person tithing. If one member broke the law, the other nine had to bring him to the monthly Hundred Court or pay a fine, and shouting the Hue and Cry forced every villager in earshot to stop work and chase a runaway thief!

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: Were Anglo-Saxon laws fair community rules or painful superstitions?
tasks.starter: Historians can see both clever community peacekeeping and painful superstition in Anglo-Saxon justice because...
hints: Give the strong case FOR fair community rules first (ten-person tithings, Hue and Cry, oath-helpers, and silver wergild stopping blood feuds).
Give the strong case FOR unfairness and superstition next (unequal shilling ranks and painful Trial by Hot Iron or Cold Water).
Reach a balanced conclusion noting that Ordeals were only used when witnesses could not agree!
tasks.model_answer: Historians can see both clever community peacekeeping and painful superstition in Anglo-Saxon justice because everyday disputes were settled sensibly, while deadlocked cases relied on luck. Ten-person tithings, the Hue and Cry, and silver wergild payments cleverly stopped violent blood feuds without prisons. However, wergild valued rich thanes above ceorl farmers, and when witnesses disagreed, Trial by Ordeal such as Trial by Hot Iron judged infection rather than real clues!

narrative_blocks.title: 1066–1150: Norman Forest Laws and Royal Fines
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.1] After **1066**, **William the Conqueror** kept Anglo-Saxon **tithings** and the **Hue and Cry**, because they caught village thieves cheaply! However, Normans ended **wergild** to families—fines now went straight into the **King’s treasury**, and nobles could demand **Trial by Combat**.

[3.2] Villagers hated William’s **Forest Laws** across places like the **New Forest**. Hunting a wild deer or cutting firewood became **poaching** [POH-ching], punished by blinding or heavy fines! Because neighbours sympathised with hungry hunters, Robin Hood ballads cheered greenwood **outlaws**.

narrative_blocks.title: 1154–1215: Henry II’s Juries and 1215 Magna Carta
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.3] From **1154**, **King Henry II** made English courts much fairer by sending travelling royal judges around counties to enforce one shared **Common Law**. Twelve local neighbours sat as a **jury** [JOOR-ee] to weigh evidence inside royal courts like the **King’s Bench**.

[3.4] Two giant changes arrived in **1215**. At **Runnymede**, **King John** sealed **Magna Carta**, promising no free person could be jailed without lawful judgment by peers. That same year, **Pope Innocent III** banned priests from **Trial by Ordeal**—making **twelve-person juries** England’s everyday standard!

narrative_blocks.title: 1100–1485: Cathedral Sanctuary, Stocks and Pillories
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.5] The medieval **Church** also held huge legal power. A fugitive who struck the bronze **Sanctuary Knocker** on **Durham Cathedral** won **37 to 40 days** of safe **sanctuary** [SANK-choo-er-ee]. That paused the **sheriff** until the fugitive chose royal trial or lifelong exile abroad!

[3.6] Meanwhile, towns shamed petty cheats in public on market day. Drunkards sat with ankles locked in low wooden **stocks**, while bakers selling underweight bread stood upright with head and hands locked in the **pillory** [PIL-uh-ree]!

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Explain what changed and what stayed the same in English law after the Norman Conquest of 1066.

hints: Name what stayed the same first (ten-person tithings and sounding the Hue and Cry).

tasks.model_answer: After 1066, William the Conqueror sensibly kept some Anglo-Saxon rules, yet he also changed English law sharply by putting royal power first. Normans kept ten-person tithings and the Hue and Cry to catch village thieves, but ended wergild to families so fines filled the King’s treasury instead—and locked up vast woods under harsh Forest Laws that punished peasant deer poaching with blinding or heavy fines!

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: How did Norman kings and medieval royal judges change English justice after 1066?
tasks.starter: Between 1066 and 1485, medieval England laid the foundations of modern courtroom trials because...
hints: Contrast harsh early Norman Forest Laws with King Henry II’s fairer courtroom reforms from 1154.
Explain how travelling judges created one shared Common Law using twelve-person juries.
Show why 1215 was doubly important (King John sealing Magna Carta AND Pope Innocent III ending Trial by Ordeal)!
tasks.model_answer: Between 1066 and 1485, medieval England laid the foundations of modern courtroom trials because royal courts replaced superstitious ordeals with evidence and juries. Although William I angered peasants with harsh Forest Laws, King Henry II sent travelling judges across England to build one shared Common Law heard by twelve-person juries. Then in 1215, King John sealed Magna Carta promising lawful trials and Pope Innocent III banned priests from Trial by Ordeal—making trial by jury England’s lasting standard!

narrative_blocks.text:
[4.1] During **Tudor** times, rising food prices, bad harvests, and fenced sheep pastures left thousands of farmworkers jobless and hungry. With only unpaid **parish constables** and night watchmen to keep order, towns feared wandering strangers called **vagrants** [VAY-gruntz] or **vagabonds**.

[4.2] Queen **Elizabeth I’s 1601 Poor Law** split poor people into two clear groups! Elderly or sick locals received helpful parish **poor relief**, whereas healthy **"sturdy beggars"** were locked in wooden stocks, **whipped behind a cart**, or sent to **Bridewell** workhouses.

narrative_blocks.title: 1605: High Treason and the Gunpowder Plot
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.3] Fierce religious divisions made rulers dread **High Treason**—plotting to kill the monarch or destroy Parliament. In **1605**, **Robert Catesby** and explosives soldier **Guy Fawkes** hid **36 barrels of gunpowder** beneath stacked firewood under the House of Lords to blow up **King James I**!

[4.4] Tipped off by the anonymous **Monteagle Letter**, royal guards searched the dark cellar before midnight on **4–5 November 1605**, catching **Guy Fawkes** holding his shuttered iron **dark lantern**! Rowed through **Traitors’ Gate**, the plotters faced terrifying public **deterrence**.

narrative_blocks.title: 1645–1736: Witchcraft Panics and Scientific Proof
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.5] Towns wheeled wooden **ducking stools** to rivers for scolding neighbours, yet **superstition** turned deadly during the **1645–1647** Civil War. In **East Anglia**, self-named **"Witchfinder General" Matthew Hopkins** charged frightened towns fees, keeping poor older women sleepless for nights until they confessed!

[4.6] Why did witch trials finally vanish? After **1660**, peace returned, the **Royal Society** promoted **science**, and calm royal judges banned unfair "swimming" tests and demanded real courtroom proof—until Parliament’s **1736 Witchcraft Act** ended witch trials for good!

narrative_blocks.title: 1700–1800: Coastal Tea Smugglers and Highwaymen
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.1] In the **1700s** across **Britain**, heavy government **import taxes** made legal **tea**, silk, and brandy expensive. Along **Cornwall** and Sussex coves, midnight **smuggling** [SMUG-ling] gangs rowed untaxed barrels ashore in secret—another **"social crime"** cheered by whole villages eager to buy cheap tea!

[5.2] Inland, dark unlit **turnpike roads**, cash-carrying **stagecoaches**, and pocket **flintlock pistols** helped mounted **highwaymen** like **Dick Turpin** (hanged at York in **1739**) shout *"Stand and deliver!"* Highwaymen vanished once **paper banknotes**, fast armed **Royal Mail coaches**, and horse patrols spread.

narrative_blocks.title: 1688–1820: 220 Capital Laws and Reluctant Juries
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.3] Wealthy **Members of Parliament** still refused to pay taxes for a national police force. Instead, landowners passed the harsh **"Bloody Code"**: by **1810**, over **220 crimes**—including stealing **five shillings** from a shop, poaching rabbits, or cutting down young trees—carried the **death penalty**!

[5.4] Yet terrifying gallows **deterrence** backfired completely! Ordinary **twelve-person juries** hated hanging hungry teenagers for tiny thefts, so kind jurors deliberately valued stolen goods under five shillings or acquitted suspects—proving Britain needed fairer laws.

narrative_blocks.title: 1787–1868: Hulks, Australia and Elizabeth Fry
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.5] Instead of hanging every thief, judges locked prisoners aboard damp **Thames prison hulks** before shipping **over 160,000** men, women, and teenagers via **transportation** to **Australia** (**1787–1868**). After an eight-month sea voyage, convicts laboured in chains building colonial roads and farms.

[5.6] Back in London’s filthy **Newgate Prison**, Quaker reformer **Elizabeth Fry** visited freezing women and children in **1813**. Opening a bright prison **school** and paid sewing rooms in **1817**, Fry proved humane **rehabilitation** [ree-huh-bil-ih-TAY-shun] beat cruelty—inspiring the **1823 Gaols Act**!

narrative_blocks.title: 1829–1856: Sir Robert Peel’s Unarmed "Bobbies"
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.1] Fast-growing **London** outgrew elderly night watchmen! After slashing over **180 hanging laws** from the Bloody Code, Home Secretary **Sir Robert Peel** passed the **1829 Metropolitan Police Act**. He sent **1,000** paid **"Peelers"** or **"Bobbies"** onto the streets from **Scotland Yard**.

[6.2] Crucially, Peel dressed his officers in **dark blue coats** and tall top hats—never red army tunics! Carrying only a wooden **truncheon** and loud wooden **rattle** rather than guns, Bobbies walked regular foot beats to **prevent crime** peacefully through **policing by consent**.

narrative_blocks.title: 1842–1965: Victorian Prisons to Abolishing Hanging
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.3] As convict **transportation** ended (**1868**), purpose-built **prisons** became Britain’s main punishment. Opened in **1842**, **Pentonville Prison** enforced the silent **Separate System** inside solitary cells alongside exhausting hard labour climbing wooden **treadwheels** or turning heavy cell cranks!

[6.4] Gradually, Victorian harshness gave way to humane reform. Britain ended public street hanging in **1868** and **abolished the death penalty** for murder in **1965**, while modern courts focus on **rehabilitation**, **youth courts**, probation, and unpaid **community payback**.

narrative_blocks.title: 1901–Present: Fingerprints, 1984 DNA and Modern Policing
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.5] Modern science transformed how detectives prove guilt fairly! In **1901**, **Scotland Yard** opened its **Fingerprint Bureau**, matching unique fingertip whorls left at crime scenes. In **1937**, **999** emergency phone calls linked citizens to fast radio patrol cars, later joined by town **CCTV**.

[6.6] Then in **1984**, **Professor Sir Alec Jeffreys** at **Leicester University** discovered genetic **DNA profiling**—identifying guilty offenders AND clearing innocent suspects from a single hair or drop of saliva! Today, **forensics** and digital **cyber-crime** teams work alongside neighbourhood officers.

key_individuals.name: King Alfred the Great (AD 849–899)
key_individuals.role: Compiler of the Written Old English Law Code (Domboc) and Champion of Wergild Peace
key_individuals.origins: Born at Wantage in AD 849 as the youngest son of King Aethelwulf of Wessex; defended Anglo-Saxon England against Viking armies before rebuilding burhs, schools, and courts.
key_individuals.significance: Gathered earlier laws of Kent, Mercia, and Wessex alongside biblical fairness principles into his landmark written Old English law book (the Domboc), strengthening peaceful wergild compensation over family blood feuds.
achievements: Compiled the Domboc ("Book of Laws") in Old English so royal reeves and Hundred Courts judged injuries consistently.
Insisted judges weigh cases fairly for rich and poor alike, backing ten-person tithings and silver wergild peacekeeping.
Trained royal officials to read and write English so written court records and charters spread across Anglo-Saxon kingdoms.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Translated and gathered laws into everyday Old English rather than Latin so local ealdormen could hear them read aloud and understood!

key_individuals.name: King Henry II (AD 1133–1189)
key_individuals.role: Architect of English Common Law, Travelling Assize Judges and Twelve-Person Juries
key_individuals.origins: Grandson of King Henry I, taking the English throne in 1154 after years of civil war ("the Anarchy") had left local courts chaotic and uneven.
key_individuals.significance: Laid the enduring foundations of the English-speaking world’s legal system by creating one unified royal "Common Law" enforced by travelling judges and twelve-person local juries.
achievements: Issued the Assize of Clarendon (1166), sending royal judges on county circuits to apply one shared Common Law across all England.
Established sworn panels of twelve local neighbours to present and weigh evidence—the direct ancestor of our modern courtroom jury!
Opened permanent royal courts at Westminster that paved the way for 1215 Magna Carta and replacing Trial by Ordeal.
key_individuals.key_distinction: More than 850 years later, Crown Courts from London to Sydney and New York still use the twelve-person jury model shaped under Henry II!

key_individuals.name: Guy Fawkes and the 1605 Conspirators (1570–1606)
key_individuals.role: Explosives Specialist Caught Guarding 36 Gunpowder Barrels in the Westminster Cellars
key_individuals.origins: Guy Fawkes was born in York in 1570 and gained military explosives experience fighting in Europe before joining Robert Catesby’s secret circle of Catholic plotters in 1604.
key_individuals.significance: Their failed plot to blow up King James I and the House of Lords became Britain’s most famous High Treason case, demonstrating early modern intelligence, physical evidence, and public deterrence.
achievements: Rented an undercroft cellar directly beneath the House of Lords and smuggled in thirty-six barrels of gunpowder hidden under firewood.
Exposed after an anonymous warning note—the Monteagle Letter—prompted Sir Thomas Knyvet’s midnight cellar search on 4–5 November 1605.
Captured carrying slow-burning fuses, a pocket watch, and the shuttered iron dark lantern still displayed at Oxford’s Ashmolean Museum!
key_individuals.key_distinction: Remembered every Bonfire Night (5 November)—and Parliament’s Yeomen of the Guard still ceremonially search the Westminster cellars before every State Opening!

key_individuals.name: Elizabeth Fry (1780–1845)
key_individuals.role: Quaker Prison Reformer Who Pioneered Humane Rehabilitation Inside Newgate Prison
key_individuals.origins: Born Elizabeth Gurney into a compassionate Quaker family in Norwich in 1780; combined raising eleven children in London with tireless charity work for the poor and imprisoned.
key_individuals.significance: Proved to a sceptical Parliament that treating prisoners as human beings—with clean clothes, female warders, schooling, and work skills—reduced reoffending far better than filthy Bloody Code cells.
achievements: Entered Newgate Prison’s overcrowded women’s ward in 1813 bringing warm flannel clothes for shivering babies and mothers.
Founded a prison school for children and paid patchwork sewing workshops inside Newgate in 1817, supervised by female matrons.
Became the first woman to give evidence to a House of Commons committee on prisons (1818), directly inspiring Robert Peel’s 1823 Gaols Act!
key_individuals.key_distinction: Inspecting convict ships too, she gave every transported woman a sewing bag of cloth and thread so she could earn honest money on arrival in Australia!

key_individuals.name: Sir Robert Peel (1788–1850)
key_individuals.role: Founder of the 1829 Metropolitan Police ("Bobbies" / "Peelers") and Penal Law Reformer
key_individuals.origins: Born in Lancashire in 1788 as the son of a wealthy cotton textile manufacturer; served as transformative Home Secretary in the 1820s before twice becoming Prime Minister.
key_individuals.significance: Dismantled most of the harsh 18th-century Bloody Code, reformed county gaols, and created Britain’s first professional, unarmed uniformed police force in 1829.
achievements: Swept away over 180 obsolete death-penalty statutes in the 1820s and passed the 1823 Gaols Act paying prison warders proper wages.
Passed the Metropolitan Police Act 1829, establishing 1,000 full-time "Bobbies" headquartered at Scotland Yard in London.
Insisted officers wear civilian-style navy coats and carry wooden truncheons rather than guns—anchoring British "policing by consent"!
key_individuals.key_distinction: Nearly two centuries later, British police officers are still affectionately called "Bobbies" after Robert Peel!

key_individuals.name: Professor Sir Alec Jeffreys (b. 1950)
key_individuals.role: British Geneticist Who Discovered Forensic DNA Fingerprinting and Profiling
key_individuals.origins: Born in Oxford in 1950—given a chemistry set and brass microscope by his father aged eight—before becoming Professor of Genetics at the University of Leicester.
key_individuals.significance: Revolutionised global crime detection and courtroom fairness in 1984 by discovering that X-ray films of human DNA revealed unique personal genetic patterns.
achievements: Had his "Eureka!" moment in his Leicester laboratory at 9:05am on Monday 10 September 1984 upon seeing unique family DNA bands.
In its very first criminal murder inquiry (1986–1987), his DNA test proved an arrested teenager was completely INNOCENT before identifying the real culprit!
Enabled police forces and innocence projects worldwide to solve cold cases and exonerate wrongly convicted prisoners from microscopic traces.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Proved that modern forensic science serves two sacred duties at once: catching the guilty AND protecting the innocent!

guided_reading.book_title: Stolen at the Baths! Docimedis's Lead Curse to Sulis Minerva
guided_reading.author: Docimedis of Aquae Sulis (Roman Baths Curse Tablet, Tabellae Sulis 10, c. AD 150–300)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Adapted into accessible Key Stage 2 English from Roman lead curse tablets (Tabellae Sulis, especially no. 10 by Docimedis and cloak curses to Sulis Minerva) excavated from the Sacred Spring at Aquae Sulis (Bath) and inscribed on thin pewter and lead sheets.
guided_reading.author_context: Without a modern police force in Roman Britain, what could an ordinary bather do when a sneak thief snatched their warm woollen cloak or gloves from the changing rooms at Bath? Read how angry citizens scratched secret messages onto lead for the goddess Sulis Minerva!
guided_reading.cover_caption: Original folded Roman lead curse tablet (defixio) scratched with Latin letters and thrown into the steaming Sacred Spring at Aquae Sulis, Bath.

vocabVault.def: The Roman spa town of Bath in Somerset, built around steaming hot mineral springs sacred to the goddess Sulis Minerva.
A thin sheet of Roman lead or pewter scratched with a plea asking a god or goddess to track down and punish a thief.
A pointed iron or bronze Roman writing pen used to scratch sharp Latin letters onto wax boards or soft lead sheets.
A senior Roman town judge who heard serious court cases inside the stone basilica hall when a suspect was caught.

guided_reading.extract: Steam curled off the green pools at Aquae Sulis as I stepped from the warm bath. I shivered in shock! My thick wool cloak and two warm gloves had vanished from the stone bench. No police officer walked Roman streets to hunt an unseen thief. A town magistrate in the court hall could only judge a suspect if I caught them myself. So I bought a thin grey sheet of soft lead and gripped a sharp iron stylus. Pressing hard, I scratched my plea to the goddess of the spring: "Goddess Sulis Minerva! Docimedis has lost two gloves and a warm cloak. Is the thief man or woman, free citizen or slave? Let them lose sleep and health until they bring my goods back to your temple!" I folded the lead sheet tight so human eyes could not read a word. Walking to the hot sacred pool, I dropped my curse into the dark water.

parent_discussion.question: Why couldn't Docimedis simply ask a Roman magistrate to investigate the missing cloak and gloves right away?
parent_discussion.answer: Roman Britain had no detective police force—victims had to catch a suspect themselves before bringing them to a magistrate's court!

parent_discussion.question: Why did Roman bathers fold their lead curse tablets tightly before dropping them into the steaming spring at Bath?
parent_discussion.answer: They folded the thin lead sheets so mortal eyes could not read the secret message meant only for the goddess Sulis Minerva!

parent_discussion.question: What does listing 'man or woman, free citizen or slave' tell us about who visited the Roman baths and who could be suspected?
parent_discussion.answer: It shows the busy baths held men, women, free citizens, and enslaved workers side by side—and Docimedis had no clue who took his things!

guided_reading.author: The History Revision Hub Narrative Archive
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original historical micro-story grounded in Anglo-Saxon Hundred Laws, King Alfred's Domboc (c. AD 890), and Textus Roffensis rules governing tithings of ten men, compulsory Hue and Cry pursuits, and silver wergild/bot compensation.
guided_reading.author_context: Imagine living in a thatched Anglo-Saxon village in AD 895 with zero police cars, zero radios, and thick oak woods all around! Discover how every neighbour over twelve had to drop their plough and sprint whenever the cow-horn sounded!

vocabVault.def: A group of ten Anglo-Saxon neighbours aged twelve and over who promised to keep one another honest and bring lawbreakers to court.
A loud alarm shouted or blown on a horn forcing every villager in earshot to stop work and chase a runaway thief immediately.
Literally 'person-price' in Old English—silver coins paid by a wrongdoer's family to an injured victim's kin to stop blood feuds.
An open-air monthly Anglo-Saxon court where local elders and witnesses settled village disputes and set silver fines.

guided_reading.extract: Frost crunched under Oslac's boots in Wiltshire around AD 895. Checking his thatched sheep pen at dawn, he gasped aloud! The wood gate hung wide open, and two plump ewes had gone. Fresh prints in the mud led straight to the oak woods. Oslac could not call a police station, for none existed in England. Instead, he raised his curved cow-horn and blew three loud blasts. Then he yelled across the fields: "Out! Out! Thief in the woods!" That cry raised the Hue and Cry. By Saxon law, all ten men in Oslac's tithing had to drop their spades at once and run! Any neighbour who hid lazily indoors faced a steep fine. Soon twelve fast neighbours trapped the shaking thief by the brook. Rather than start a blood feud with swords, they led him to the open-air Hundred Court. There village elders made his kin give back both sheep and pay silver wergild coins!

parent_discussion.question: What happened to an Anglo-Saxon villager who heard the 'Hue and Cry' horn but stayed indoors instead of helping chase the thief?
parent_discussion.answer: Their whole tithing or household faced a strict silver fine because chasing thieves was every neighbour's legal duty!

parent_discussion.question: How did grouping everyone aged twelve and over into a ten-person 'tithing' stop lots of crimes before they even started?
parent_discussion.answer: If one member broke the law and ran away, the other nine neighbours had to bring them to court or pay the fine themselves!

parent_discussion.question: Why was paying silver 'wergild' compensation wiser for a small village than letting angry families take revenge with swords?
parent_discussion.answer: Revenge killings started endless blood feuds between neighbours, whereas agreed silver compensation restored peace safely.

story_check.question: At what age did Anglo-Saxon boys join a local ten-person 'tithing' responsible for keeping the peace?
story_check.feedback: Spot on! From age twelve, every male villager belonged to a tithing of ten neighbours who answered for one another's behaviour.

story_check.question: What did the Old English word 'wergild' literally mean?
options: Person-price (silver compensation paid to stop family blood feuds)
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! 'Wer' meant person and 'gild' meant payment or price—fixing exact silver sums for every injury.

story_check.question: What had to happen the moment someone shouted the 'Hue and Cry' in an Anglo-Saxon village?
options: Everyone locked their doors and hid under beds
Only paid uniformed police officers chased the suspect
Every villager within earshot had to stop work immediately and join the chase
Villagers wrote a letter to Rome and waited six months
story_check.feedback: Well remembered! Community policing relied on every single neighbour dropping tools to track the suspect together.

monday_cold_call.question: How did Anglo-Saxon 'tithings', the 'Hue and Cry', and 'wergild' keep villages peaceful without a police force?
monday_cold_call.answer: Ten-person tithings watched neighbours' behaviour, everyone had to chase thieves during the Hue and Cry, and silver wergild fines stopped revenge feuds.

guided_reading.hinge_question: Why did community policing like the Hue and Cry work well in tiny villages of 100 people, yet struggle centuries later in huge cities?

guided_reading.book_title: A Gest of Robyn Hode (Outlaws in the King's Royal Forest)
guided_reading.author: Traditional Medieval English Ballad (First Printed c. 1495, Public Domain)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Public-domain medieval ballad lines adapted into clear modern spelling from 'A Gest of Robyn Hode' (c. 1450–1495, Child Ballad 117), paired with historical context on Norman Forest Laws and medieval outlaws.
guided_reading.author_context: After 1066, Norman kings fenced off huge woodlands under harsh Forest Laws—making it a terrible crime for hungry villagers to hunt wild deer! Read aloud from England's oldest Robin Hood ballad to hear why ordinary folk cheered a greenwood outlaw!
guided_reading.cover_caption: Wild fallow deer beneath ancient oaks in the New Forest — strictly reserved for royal hunting under Norman Forest Laws after 1066.

vocabVault.def: Harsh Norman laws brought in by William the Conqueror forbidding villagers from hunting royal deer or chopping wood without pay.
A fugitive placed completely 'outside the law' after fleeing court—anyone could capture them, so many hid in deep forests.
From 'shire-reeve'—the king's chief county officer who collected taxes, hunted outlaws, and guarded royal castles.
Secretly hunting deer, rabbits, or fish on land claimed by the king or wealthy lords—seen by many villagers as a 'social crime'.

guided_reading.extract: After 1066, Norman kings claimed wide English woods for royal sport. Taking one wild deer became poaching, punished by grim fines! Men who fled court were named outlaws and hid among tall green oaks. By winter fires, folk sang of a bold archer who tricked the greedy Sheriff: "Listen close, good neighbours all, of freeborn country blood! I shall tell you of a brave archer, his name was Robin Hood. Robin stood in green Barnsdale, and leaned against a tree. Beside him stood tall Little John, a loyal friend was he." Robin gave Little John one firm rule before they walked the woods: "Never harm an honest farmer, who ploughs the muddy ground! Never rob a kindly yeoman, walking where green trees grow round. Greedy lords and unfair judges, bind their purses tight! And watch the Sheriff of Nottingham, by morning and by night!"

parent_discussion.question: In the medieval ballad, which hardworking country people did Robin Hood strictly forbid Little John from harming?
parent_discussion.answer: Hardworking farmers ploughing the ground and ordinary country yeomen walking through the greenwood!

parent_discussion.question: Why did ordinary medieval villagers resent William the Conqueror's 'Forest Laws' so deeply?
parent_discussion.answer: Woods where families had gathered firewood and hunted food for generations were suddenly locked up for royal deer hunting under cruel punishments.

parent_discussion.question: Even if Robin Hood himself was a legend, what real historical feelings do medieval Robin Hood ballads reveal to historians?
parent_discussion.answer: They prove how strongly ordinary medieval people hated unfair taxes, corrupt sheriffs, and harsh Forest Laws!

story_check.question: What did being declared a medieval 'outlaw' actually mean?
options: You were promoted to judge in the King's court
You were placed 'outside the law's protection' for fleeing trial, forcing many fugitives into woods
You were given a free royal deer every Christmas
You wore a blue police uniform in London
story_check.feedback: Spot on! Anyone who refused three court summonses was placed outside the law, losing all legal safety.

story_check.question: Who did Robin Hood tell Little John to keep firmly in mind as their main rival in the ballad?
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! As the king's chief county tax collector and law officer, the Sheriff was the ballad's classic villain.

story_check.question: Why can legends like 'A Gest of Robyn Hode' still be useful clues for careful historians?
options: They prove every single word of Robin's adventures happened on camera
They reveal ordinary medieval villagers' real anger toward harsh Forest Laws and unfair sheriffs
They list modern DNA laboratory rules
They were written by Norman kings to praise deer poaching
story_check.feedback: Well remembered! Even folk ballads reveal real medieval attitudes toward justice, fair play, and royal Forest Laws.

monday_cold_call.question: Why did Norman Forest Laws make legends like 'Robin Hood' so popular among medieval English villagers?
monday_cold_call.answer: Norman Forest Laws banned villagers from hunting deer or gathering wood under harsh penalties, so songs about an outlaw outwitting greedy sheriffs thrilled ordinary folk.

guided_reading.hinge_question: Why do historians call poaching royal deer a 'social crime'—a crime on paper that neighbours often refused to report?

guided_reading.book_title: Thirty-Six Barrels in the Dark: Catching Guy Fawkes on 5 November 1605
guided_reading.author: The History Revision Hub Narrative Archive
guided_reading.provenance_note: Original historical micro-story grounded in the anonymous Monteagle Letter (26 October 1605, The National Archives SP 14/216/2), Sir Thomas Knyvet's midnight Westminster search, and Guy Fawkes's iron lantern preserved in the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford.
guided_reading.author_context: High treason—plotting to kill the monarch or blow up Parliament—was the most terrifying crime in Tudor and Stuart Britain! Creep down into the pitch-black cellar beneath the House of Lords just before midnight on 4–5 November 1605!
guided_reading.cover_caption: The real sheet-iron dark lantern held by Guy Fawkes when guards seized him beneath Parliament on 5 November 1605 (Ashmolean Museum).

vocabVault.def: The most serious crime in the kingdom: plotting to overthrow or kill the king or queen or destroy Parliament.
An iron candle lantern with a sliding metal shutter that hid its flame instantly in dark cellars—like Guy Fawkes's 1605 lantern.
A mysterious unsigned note delivered in October 1605 warning Lord Monteagle to stay away from Parliament before a 'terrible blow'.
Making punishments deliberately frightening in public so other people are too scared to copy the crime.

guided_reading.extract: Ten days before King James I opened Parliament, a stranger handed a secret note to Lord Monteagle. "Stay away!" the unsigned Monteagle Letter warned. "Parliament shall receive a terrible blow, yet they shall not see who hurts them!" Clever King James guessed at once what "a terrible blow" meant. He ordered guards to check for gunpowder! Near midnight on 4 November 1605, Sir Thomas Knyvet led armed men into a dark cellar right below the House of Lords. By a pile of wood stood a tall man in riding boots calling himself "John Johnson". His real name was Guy Fawkes! In his hand shone an iron dark lantern with a sliding cover. In his coat lay a watch and slow fuses. Guards pulled the firewood aside and gasped! Thirty-six barrels of black powder sat waiting to blow the hall sky-high. Caught in high treason, the plotters faced harsh public deterrence.

parent_discussion.question: Which clue inside the anonymous Monteagle Letter helped King James I guess that plotters planned an explosion?
parent_discussion.answer: The warning that Parliament would 'receive a terrible blow... yet they shall not see who hurts them' pointed straight to hidden gunpowder!

parent_discussion.question: Why did Guy Fawkes carry a special 'dark lantern' with a sliding iron cover instead of an open flaming torch?
parent_discussion.answer: A sliding shutter hid the light from guards AND kept naked sparks safely away from thirty-six barrels of explosive gunpowder!

parent_discussion.question: Why did Tudor and Stuart rulers punish 'high treason' more fiercely and publicly than any other crime?
parent_discussion.answer: With no national police or standing army, monarchs used terrifying public deterrence to scare anyone else away from rebellion.

story_check.question: What fake name did Guy Fawkes give when royal guards first stopped him in the Westminster cellar?
story_check.feedback: Spot on! Posing as a servant named 'John Johnson', Fawkes guarded thirty-six hidden barrels of gunpowder.

story_check.question: How many barrels of gunpowder had Robert Catesby's plotters hidden beneath stacked firewood under the House of Lords?
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! Thirty-six barrels held enough black powder to shatter the House of Lords and nearby Westminster buildings.

story_check.question: Where can visitors today still inspect the real sheet-iron lantern seized from Guy Fawkes on 5 November 1605?
options: Inside the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford
At the bottom of the River Thames
story_check.feedback: Well remembered! Fawkes's iron dark lantern has been preserved at Oxford since 1641 as primary physical evidence.

monday_cold_call.question: How was the 1605 Gunpowder Plot uncovered, and what physical items were found on Guy Fawkes beneath Westminster?
monday_cold_call.answer: The anonymous Monteagle Letter alerted King James I; guards searching the cellar found 36 gunpowder barrels plus Fawkes's dark lantern, watch, and fuses.

guided_reading.hinge_question: Why does Guy Fawkes's real iron lantern in Oxford make the 1605 plot feel more real than a storybook picture?

guided_reading.book_title: Straw, Cold Stone and Hope: Elizabeth Fry Enters Newgate Prison (1813)
guided_reading.author: Elizabeth Fry & Anna Buxton (Adapted from Newgate Prison Journals, 1813–1817, Public Domain)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Adapted into accessible Key Stage 2 English from Quaker reformer Elizabeth Fry's public-domain journals and 'Observations on the Visiting, Superintendence, and Government of Female Prisoners' (1827).
guided_reading.author_context: Under the harsh 18th-century 'Bloody Code', damp prisons like London's Newgate crammed hundreds of awaiting-trial suspects, debtors, and children together onto filthy straw! Step inside Newgate with Quaker reformer Elizabeth Fry in 1813!
guided_reading.cover_caption: Portrait engraving of Quaker prison reformer Elizabeth Fry (1780–1845), who founded a school and sewing workshops inside Newgate Prison.

vocabVault.def: London's grim, overcrowded stone prison where men, women, and children awaited trial, hanging, or convict ships to Australia.
Helping prisoners reform through clean rooms, reading lessons, and paid work skills so they can live honestly after release.
Members of the Christian Religious Society of Friends—like Elizabeth Fry—who believed every human being deserved kindness and dignity.
Shipping over 160,000 British convicts in chains across the ocean to work in Australian penal colonies between 1787 and 1868.

guided_reading.extract: Guards told me to leave my watch outside before opening the heavy gate at Newgate Prison in winter 1813. Nearly three hundred women and small children crowded into four damp stone rooms! Women facing transportation ships to Australia slept next to mothers who had not yet seen a judge. Most had no beds and no warm blankets against the icy stone floor. Little babies shivered in thin rags. My fellow Quakers and I did not shout at them. We stitched warm wool clothes for the children and spoke to each woman with kind respect. Back in 1817, I asked the mothers a gentle question. "Even behind these dark bars, will you help us start a school for your children?" Tears of hope shone on tired faces as every mother agreed! Soon women learned to read and sew neat quilts to sell. Kindness and real skills proved rehabilitation worked.

parent_discussion.question: What shocked Elizabeth Fry most about how prisoners were mixed together inside Newgate's women's ward in 1813?
parent_discussion.answer: Convicted prisoners awaiting transportation slept crammed into four freezing rooms alongside unconvicted women and little children!

parent_discussion.question: Why did Elizabeth Fry ask the women's permission to start a prison school and sewing work instead of simply barking orders?
parent_discussion.answer: Treating prisoners with dignity and letting them agree to their own fair rules gave them pride, hope, and real self-respect.

parent_discussion.question: What is the big difference between 'deterrence' under the Bloody Code and 'rehabilitation' taught by Elizabeth Fry?
parent_discussion.answer: Deterrence tries to terrify people with harsh punishments, whereas rehabilitation teaches reading and job skills so prisoners can rebuild honest lives.

story_check.question: Which London prison did Quaker reformer Elizabeth Fry famously visit and transform from 1813–1817?
story_check.feedback: Spot on! Elizabeth Fry's Newgate school and sewing rooms amazed Members of Parliament and inspired the 1823 Gaols Act.

story_check.question: Which practical skills did Elizabeth Fry help women and children learn inside Newgate Prison?
options: Reading, schooling for children, and patchwork needlework they could sell
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! Reading and sewing gave women honest skills and small earnings so they did not have to steal when freed.

story_check.question: What did 'transportation' mean for over 160,000 British prisoners between 1787 and 1868?
options: Riding a free Royal Mail stagecoach to Scotland
Being shipped across the ocean to work in Australian convict colonies
Walking to the next village market
Patrolling London streets in a top hat
story_check.feedback: Well remembered! After Britain lost American colonies, convict ships carried prisoners on long voyages to Australia.

monday_cold_call.question: What terrible conditions did Elizabeth Fry find inside Newgate Prison in 1813, and how did she prove 'rehabilitation' worked?
monday_cold_call.answer: Nearly 300 women and children slept on freezing stone without beds; Fry opened a prison school, provided clean clothes, and taught paid sewing.

guided_reading.hinge_question: Why was Elizabeth Fry's portrait later printed on Britain's five-pound note for fifteen years?

guided_reading.book_title: A Study in Scarlet (Sherlock Holmes Inspects Tiny Clues, 1887)
guided_reading.author: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle (Published 1887, Public Domain)
guided_reading.provenance_note: Public-domain literary extract adapted for Key Stage 2 sentence length from Sir Arthur Conan Doyle's 'A Study in Scarlet' (Chapter 3, 1887), illustrating late-Victorian fascination with scientific crime-scene observation ahead of Scotland Yard's 1901 Fingerprint Bureau.
guided_reading.author_context: Before 1900, real police detectives were only just learning to guard crime scenes and study footprints, dust, and fingerprints! Read Sir Arthur Conan Doyle's famous 1887 story to watch Sherlock Holmes amaze Dr Watson with a magnifying glass and tape measure!
guided_reading.cover_caption: Close-up of unique raised friction-ridge whorls on a fingertip — adopted by Scotland Yard's Fingerprint Bureau in 1901 just fourteen years after Sherlock Holmes debuted!

vocabVault.def: Using careful scientific tests—such as fingerprints, microscopes, and DNA—to solve crimes fairly with physical proof.
Working out what happened step by step from tiny physical clues rather than guessing or relying on rumours.
The unique loops, arches, and whorls on each person's fingertips—first used by Scotland Yard's Fingerprint Bureau in 1901.
The 1984 Leicester breakthrough by Sir Alec Jeffreys reading unique genetic code from tiny drops of blood, hair, or saliva.

guided_reading.extract: In 1887, doctor Arthur Conan Doyle thrilled readers with a sharp new detective named Sherlock Holmes. Holmes trusted real clues and forensics far above guesswork! Watch Dr Watson describe Holmes checking a dusty London room. "As he spoke, he whipped a tape measure and a round glass lens from his coat pocket. With those two tools he stepped softly round the room. Sometimes he stopped still or knelt low. Once he even lay flat upon the dusty boards! He grew so busy with his search that he forgot we stood there. Under his breath he gave little cries and whistles of joy. For twenty minutes he worked on with the utmost care. He measured faint boot marks unseen to my eyes. Then he checked every tiny scratch along the walls!" Fourteen years later, Scotland Yard opened its real Fingerprint Bureau!

parent_discussion.question: Which two simple scientific tools did Sherlock Holmes pull from his pocket to examine the dusty room?
parent_discussion.answer: A tape measure and a round magnifying lens!

parent_discussion.question: How is Sherlock Holmes's careful search for unseen boot marks the exact opposite of Anglo-Saxon 'Trial by Ordeal' or 1640s witch trials?
parent_discussion.answer: Ordeals and witch trials relied on superstition and painful tests, whereas forensic detectives measure real physical clues left at the scene!

parent_discussion.question: Which two real British scientific breakthroughs in 1901 and 1984 turned Sherlock Holmes's dream of scientific proof into everyday policing?
parent_discussion.answer: Scotland Yard's Fingerprint Bureau in 1901 and Sir Alec Jeffreys's discovery of DNA profiling at Leicester in 1984!

story_check.question: Who wrote the famous Victorian detective story 'A Study in Scarlet' in 1887?
story_check.feedback: Spot on! Trained as a medical doctor in Edinburgh, Conan Doyle inspired real police scientists worldwide.

story_check.question: In 1901—just fourteen years after Sherlock Holmes first appeared—what scientific unit opened at London's Scotland Yard?
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! Because no two people share identical fingertip ridges, fingerprints gave courts reliable physical proof.

story_check.question: Which 1984 University of Leicester breakthrough can clear innocent suspects as well as identify guilty offenders?
options: DNA profiling (discovered by Professor Sir Alec Jeffreys)
story_check.feedback: Well remembered! Sir Alec Jeffreys's DNA profiling transformed modern justice both by catching offenders and freeing innocent people.

monday_cold_call.question: How did Sherlock Holmes's magnifying-glass clues point forward to real British forensic breakthroughs in 1901 and 1984?
monday_cold_call.answer: Holmes championed measuring tiny physical clues; soon Scotland Yard opened its Fingerprint Bureau (1901) and Sir Alec Jeffreys discovered DNA profiling (1984).

guided_reading.hinge_question: Why is clearing an innocent suspect with DNA just as important for fair justice as catching a guilty criminal?

glossary.definition: The Roman spa town of Bath in Somerset, where bathers dropped over 130 scratched lead curse tablets into Sulis Minerva’s hot spring.
Travelling royal courts set up by King Henry II where royal judges rode round English counties to hear serious cases before local juries.
Nickname for harsh 18th-century British laws that punished over 220 crimes—even stealing five shillings or chopping down trees—by hanging.
Popular nickname (alongside "Peelers") for London’s first uniformed Metropolitan Police officers, named after founder Sir Robert Peel in 1829.
One shared royal law for all England introduced under King Henry II, replacing patchwork local customs with consistent judge and jury rules.
A thin folded sheet of Roman lead (defixio) scratched with Latin letters begging a god or goddess to track down and punish an unknown thief.
Designing harsh or public punishments—like village stocks or treason executions—to frighten onlookers so nobody dares copy the crime.
Genetic forensic test discovered in 1984 by Professor Sir Alec Jeffreys in Leicester, matching unique DNA from tiny traces of blood, hair, or saliva.
A wooden chair fixed to the end of a long see-saw beam used in Tudor and Stuart towns to dunk accused scolds or dishonest bakers into cold river water.
Unique patterns of loops, arches, and whorls on human fingertips, adopted by London’s Scotland Yard Fingerprint Bureau in 1901 to solve crimes.
Strict Norman laws created by William the Conqueror after 1066 banning ordinary villagers from hunting wild deer or cutting wood in royal forests.
Scientific crime-solving methods—including fingerprints, microscope fibres, ballistics, and DNA—used to prove guilt or clear innocent suspects.
Betraying or plotting to kill the monarch or blow up Parliament—such as the 1605 Gunpowder Plot—treated as the most serious crime in Britain.
An armed robber on horseback in the 1700s—like Dick Turpin—who held up slow stagecoaches along unlit roads with flintlock pistols.
An Anglo-Saxon and medieval alarm shouted or blown on a horn requiring every villager within earshot to stop work and chase a suspect at once.
A group of twelve sworn citizens who listen carefully to courtroom evidence and witnesses before deciding fairly whether a suspect is guilty or innocent.
A Roman or modern local judge who hears court cases, weighs witness statements, and decides lawful fines or sentences.
The "Great Charter" sealed by King John at Runnymede in 1215, promising that even the king must obey the law and free citizens deserve a fair trial.

Secretly hunting deer, rabbits, or pheasants on royal or landowner estates—seen by many hungry villagers as a "social crime".
An old dismasted wooden warship moored on rivers like the Thames to hold overcrowded convicts in damp chains before transportation.
Helping offenders change their lives for good through clean prisons, schooling, and work skills—championed at Newgate by Elizabeth Fry.
Medieval Church protection lasting up to 37–40 days for any fugitive who struck a cathedral door knocker, pausing arrest before trial or exile.
Secretly landing untaxed goods like tea, silk, and brandy onto dark beaches at night to dodge heavy 18th-century government customs taxes.
An Anglo-Saxon group of ten local males aged twelve and over who promised to keep one another honest or bring lawbreakers to court.
Sending over 160,000 convicted British prisoners by ship between 1787 and 1868 to serve hard-labour sentences in Australian colonies.
An Anglo-Saxon and early medieval church test—using red-hot iron or cold water—asking God to show guilt or innocence when witnesses could not agree.
Old English for "person-price"—a fixed sum of silver coins paid by a wrongdoer’s family to an injured victim’s kin to stop violent blood feuds.
